Experiment 01 · Hotspot persistence

Does recorded hotspot activity persist?

Purpose: test whether recent hotspot observations help predict a detection in the same area the next day, and establish a benchmark for future graph models.

Quiet is not the negative class

Quiet/active describes the previous seven days; positive/negative describes the target day. To predict August 15, quiet means no recorded detections during August 8–14 in the relevant area.

Class-imbalance technique: step by step

Selective random undersampling, followed by a sampling correction to scores. Applied in Experiments 03–04; not in persistence Experiments 01–02.

  1. Select training rows: keep every positive and every active row. Give each quiet negative a 1% chance of being retained. This is not sampling 1% of all negatives or making a 50/50 dataset.
  2. Train without class weights: Experiment 03 uses the saved sampled rows. Experiment 04 keeps the full graph, but uses a fresh quiet-negative sample in the training loss each step.
  3. Correct quiet-row scores: sampling makes positives appear more common among quiet examples. At prediction time, multiply predicted odds by 0.01 for every quiet row; active-row scores are unchanged. This uses past-history quiet status, never the unknown target label.
  4. Evaluate on all rows: apply the correction before selecting thresholds on 2022 and evaluating on 2023. Evaluation data is not undersampled.

Why correct the scores? An illustrative example

  • Suppose the original quiet training group has 100 positives and 10,000 negatives: its positive rate is 100 / 10,100 ≈ 0.99%.
  • Keeping all 100 positives and approximately 1% of negatives leaves 100 positives and about 100 negatives: roughly 50% positive in the sample.
  • The population did not change; sampling changed what the model saw. The correction accounts for this difference.

For an illustrative quiet-row prediction of 50%:

Original odds      = 0.50 / (1 - 0.50) = 1
Corrected odds     = 1 × 0.01 = 0.01
Corrected probability = 0.01 / (1 + 0.01) ≈ 0.99%

Code equivalent: corrected log-odds = model log-odds + log(0.01)

0.01 comes from the 1% negative-retention probability. It is not a buffer, clipping threshold, or training weight. This corrects the sampling-induced odds shift; it does not guarantee calibrated probabilities from a fitted model. No separate probability-calibration procedure has been fitted.

  • Positive means at least one recorded hotspot detection. A zero target means no recorded detection, not verified absence of fire; observation coverage remains unknown.
  • BC totals count region–cell–days. Border cells may appear in multiple regional grids; these are not deduplicated province-wide cell-days.
  • Heavy imbalance makes accuracy alone misleading; interpret precision, recall, F1 and average precision alongside the positive prevalence.

01 / Spatial evidence: recurring areas of activity

  • We inspected Kamloops in 2018 and 2023, first monthly, then through four August periods.
  • Clusters recur in similar areas across panels. This suggests spatial persistence; maps alone do not identify the same fires or prove spread.

August 22–31 contains 10 days; the other periods contain 7. Raw totals are not equal-duration comparisons. Weekly maps share one colour scale across both years.

Selected rule: a detection in the same cell yesterday → predict a detection today.
  • Example: to predict August 15, the 1-day rule uses August 14; the 3-day rule uses August 12–14; the 7-day rule uses August 8–14.
  • Rule, not a trained model: predict 1 when the past count exceeds zero. No GNN or learned weights yet.
  • Split: 2018–2021 diagnostics → compare fixed rules on 2022 → select highest F1 → evaluate on 2023.
  • Scope: 16,233 fixed cells; May 8–September 30 targets; seven-day warmup omitted; all cells retained.

  • Adding yesterday’s neighbour activity: recall rises to 80.2%, while precision falls to 23.7%.
  • Context: only 0.161% of all evaluated cell-days had recorded detections.

04 / Conclusion

  • Spatial plots suggested recurring locations; the baseline quantified day-to-day persistence.
  • Recent same-cell activity is a useful signal. Broader neighbour rules catch more activity at the cost of more false positives.
  • Future learned models and GNNs should improve on this benchmark under the same evaluation setup.
  • Counts and targets describe recorded observations, not ignition, unique fires, severity or confirmed fire absence. Coverage remains unknown.
  • 2023 is a development evaluation because its plots were already inspected; 2024 remains excluded.
  • Past-only feature checks and count reconciliation passed. Prior-day records are assumed available; operational publication delays are not modeled.
